'''''Malva neglecta''''' is a species of plant of the family [[Malvaceae]], native to most of the Old World except [[sub-Saharan Africa]]. It is an annual growing to 0.6 m (2 ft). It is known as '''common mallow''' in the United States and also as '''buttonweed''', '''cheeseplant''', '''cheeseweed''', '''dwarf mallow''', and '''roundleaf mallow'''.<ref name="ITIS">{{ITIS |id=21836 |taxon=Malva neglecta |access-date=9 May 2008}}</ref>
This plant is often consumed as a food, with its leaves, stalks and seed all being considered edible.<ref>Facciola S. Cornucopia – A Source Book of Edible Plants.  Vista, Ca.  Kampong Publications, 1990. 677 p.</ref><ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211211/bdGAUejE8BM Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20140626063406/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bdGAUejE8BM&feature=channel_page Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite AV media| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bdGAUejE8BM&feature=channel_page| title = Wild Living with Sunny: Episode 16 - Mallow Plant S'mores | website=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Malva+neglecta|title=Malva neglecta Dwarf Mallow, Common mallow PFAF Plant Database}}</ref>  This is especially true of the seeds, which contain 21% protein and 15.2% fat.<ref>Duke JA.  CRC Handbook of Proximate Analysis Tables of Higher Plants. Boca Raton, Fl. CRC Press, 1986. 389 p.</ref>

==Description==
Dwarf mallow is a prostrate, downy, [[herbaceous]] plant, growing to approximately {{convert|60|cm|abbr=on}}.
The leaves are alternate with long, strongly channeled [[petiole (botany)|petioles]], up to {{convert|12|cm|abbr=on}}, and narrowly triangular [[stipules]].
It is a [[broadleaf weeds|broadleaf]] winter [[annual plant|annual]] that also persists through a [[biennial plant|biennial]] or [[perennial]] life cycle if environmental conditions are favorable.<ref>{{cite report

 |publisher=Purdue University
 |url=https://www.purduelandscapereport.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Spotlight-on-Weeds-Common-Mallow-Malva-neglecta.pdf
 |access-date=2026-01-25
}}</ref><ref>{{cite report
 |last1=Donaldson

 |publisher=University of Nevada Cooperative Extension
 |url=https://naes.agnt.unr.edu/PMS/Pubs/2020-3397.pdf
 |access-date=2026-01-25
}}</ref>
Each leaf is [[glossary of leaf morphology#reniform|reniform]] or with 5–7 shallow lobes, the [[basal (anatomy)|basal]] leaves are {{convert|3–7|cm|abbr=on}}.
It grows a tough taproot.<ref>{{cite book

The flowers are single-stalked and occur in clusters of 2–5 in the leaf [[axils]].
The flower stalks are shorter than the leaf stalks, with the leaves partially obscuring the flowers.
The fruits are [[schizocarp]]s, which split into 10–12 mericarps (nutlets) and are smooth and hairy.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref>

In addition to daily [[phototropic]] movements, leaves show [[epinasty]], [[geotropism]] and sleeping behaviors. Leaves joined to the stem on the east side of the plant bend [[wiktionary:abaxial|abaxially]] and leaves on the west side of the plant bend [[wiktionary:adaxial|adaxially]], while leaves on the north and south sides turn sideways. Overnight, leaves were observed returning to their morning position.<ref>{{cite journal

 |year=1938
 |doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1938.tb09178.x
}}</ref>

[[File:Frosted Common Mallow in Port Edward.jpg|thumb|Frost tolerance seen in Canada]]
After [[introduced species|introduction]] into [[Canada]], common mallow was found to be [[freezing tolerance|freezing tolerant]], retaining the capacity for
[[photosynthesis]] and [[Cellular respiration|respiration]] after long periods of exposure to [[freezing air temperature|subfreezing temperatures]].<ref>{{cite journal

==Life cycle==
Malva neglecta exhibits six age states: seedlings, juveniles, immatures, virginals, young generatives, and middle-aged generatives. Seedling leaf blades are [[Trichome#Aerial surface hairs|pubescent]] below and along the edge. Juvenile plants have a solitary shoot and rounded leaves with [[crenate|wavy toothed]] edges. Immature plants show kidney-shaped leaves with jagged edges. Virginile plants present [[rosette (botany)|rosettes]] of 3-5 rounded heart-shaped leaves. Young generative plants develop solitary white or light pink flowers. Branching of the generative shoot is observed in Middle-aged plants.<ref>{{cite conference
 |last=Saribaeva
 |first=Shakhnoza
 |title=Morphological variability and vitality of the cenopopulation of ''Malva neglecta'' Wallr.
 |conference=E3S Web of Conferences, SDEA-2024
 |date=13 June 2024
 |doi=10.1051/e3sconf/202453705024
 |url=https://doi.org/10.1051/e3sconf/202453705024
}}</ref>
While young leaves and stems are green, mature leaves and lower stems vary from green to purple in color.<ref>{{cite book

== Uses ==
The plant has [[1-Octacosanol]],<ref name="Dr. Dukes p">{{Cite web |title=Plant Malva neglecta (Malvaceae) {{!}} Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases |url=https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/plant-malva-neglecta |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=phytochem.nal.usda.gov}}</ref> [[Ascorbic (acid)]], [[Choline]],<ref name="Dr. Dukes p" />  alkaloids, and saponin (the plant has a certain antioxidant content).<ref>{{Cite web |title=PHYTOCHEMICAL  SCREENING  OF  SOME  SPECIES  OF  IRANIAN  PLANTS (KURDISTAN  PROVINCE ) |url=http://www.ijpr-online.com/Docs/20032/IJPR122.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040810051509/http://www.ijpr-online.com/Docs/20032/IJPR122.htm |archive-date=2004-08-10 |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=www.ijpr-online.com}}</ref> It has a high nitrate content, similar to that of [[Eruca sativa|arugula]].<ref name="PFAF">{{Cite web |title=BPB : Vol. 27  (2004)  , No. 5   702 |url=http://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/bpb/27/5/27_702/_article |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080303005040/http://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/bpb/27/5/27_702/_article |archive-date=2008-03-03 |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=www.jstage.jst.go.jp}}</ref><ref name="poi">Anthony P. Knight, Richard G. Walter: ''Guide to Plant Poisoning of Animals in North America.'' Teton NewMedia, 2001, {{ISBN|978-1-893441-11-8}}. S. 28.</ref> The flowers contain [[tannins]].

===Therapeutic===
A common traditionally used medicinal plant, used for [[catarrh]], [[enteritis]], [[sore throat]], [[hoarse voice]], and as an expectorant.<ref name="Dr. Dukes e">{{Cite web |title=Ethnobotanical Plant Malva neglecta {{!}} Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases |url=https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/ethnobotanical-plant-malva-neglecta |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=phytochem.nal.usda.gov}}</ref>
A lab study has shown that the plant is good for stomach ulcers<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gürbüz |first=Ilhan |last2=Ozkan |first2=Ayse Mine |last3=Yesilada |first3=Erdem |last4=Kutsal |first4=Osman |date=2005-10-03 |title=Anti-ulcerogenic activity of some plants used in folk medicine of Pinarbasi (Kayseri, Turkey) |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16085377 |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=101 |issue=1-3 |pages=313–318 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2005.05.015 |issn=0378-8741 |pmid=16085377}}</ref>

===Seeds===
The seeds can be eaten raw or cooked and have a nutty flavor.<ref name="PFAF" /> Mature seeds can be cooked like rice or grains.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>
In the past, seeds were ground into flour in times of need.<ref>{{Cite web |title=LNVL - Regulus - Wilde Mehllieferanten |url=https://www.luxnatur.lu/regulus/r20000410.htm |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=www.luxnatur.lu}}</ref>

===Root===
The root can be ground and used as a [[meringue]] substitute<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Facciola
 |first=Stephen
 |title=Cornucopia: A Source Book of Edible Plants
 |publisher=Kampong Publications
 |year=1990
 |location=Vista, California
 |isbn=978-0961018412
}}</ref>
by boiling in water, simmering until thickened, and then whisked like egg whites.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Malva neglecta
 |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=malva+neglecta
 |website=Plants For A Future
 |access-date=2026-01-27
}}</ref>

===Leaves===
Leaves are useful in salads, can be eaten raw, and contain Vitamin C, significant protein and mineral content.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Özer
 |first1=M.
 |last2=Aksoy
 |first2=M.
 |title=Mineral composition and nutritional properties of ''Malva neglecta'' and ''Malvella sherardiana'' consumed as vegetable in Central Black Sea Region of Turkey
 |journal=Turkish Journal of Food and Agriculture Sciences
 |date=2019-06-30
 |volume=1
 |issue=1
 |pages=18–23
 |issn=2687-3818
 |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/822815
}}</ref>
In culinary applications, it is cooked similar to [[spinach]], or used for thickening soups, as the leaves release a [[thickening agent]] similar to [[okra]] which is also in the mallow family. In [[Morocco]] leaves are known as ''Bakola'' or ''Khobiza'', braised as a [[side dish]] (called salad, but cooked) or used as a sauce over [[couscous]].<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Powell
 | first1 = Bronwen
 | last2 = Ouarghidi

 | last3 = Johns
 | first3 = Timothy
 | last4 = Ibn Tattou
 | first4 = Mohamed
 | last5 = Eyzaguirre
 | first5 = Pablo
 | title = Wild leafy vegetable use and knowledge across multiple sites in Morocco: a case study for transmission of local knowledge
 | journal = Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine
 | volume = 10
 | year = 2014
 | article-number = 34
 | pmid = 24708730
 | pmc = 4008438
 | doi = 10.1186/1746-4269-10-34
 | doi-access = free}}</ref>
In [[jewish cuisine|Jewish]] and [[egyptian cuisine|Egyptian]] cooking, leaves are made into a [[stew]] called [[Mulukhiyah]].
